blogs.title: Threats, Psychological Harm, and the Elusive Boundary of 'Persecution' in the Tenth Circuit
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Tenth Circuit's determination that threats and emotional or psychological harm—even when accumulated—do not rise to the level of persecution under the INA. It examines the tension between the cumulative-harm doctrine, which requires courts to consider incidents collectively rather than in isolation, and the court's consistent refusal to grant asylum based on threats alone. The post also discusses the practical implications for applicants who face serious but non-physical harm, and whether the Tenth Circuit's persecution threshold has become functionally impossible to meet without physical injury.

blogs.title: Mixed Motives and the 'Central Reason' Test: When Political Activity Isn't Enough for Nexus
blogs.description: This post examines the court's nexus analysis, where it concluded that the petitioners' political opinion was merely 'tangential and subordinate' to a personal property dispute with a narco-trafficker. It explores the doctrinal challenge of establishing nexus in mixed-motive cases under the 'at least one central reason' standard, particularly when applicants have genuine political involvement but are targeted primarily for personal or professional reasons. The post considers how courts disentangle protected and unprotected motives, and what this case reveals about the practical difficulty of proving political-opinion-based persecution when private actors have multiple incentives for targeting an applicant.

blogs.title: Individual Apathy vs. Systemic Failure: The Reporting Requirement in 'Unable or Unwilling' Analysis
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Tenth Circuit's treatment of the government-protection prong, focusing on the court's distinction between isolated encounters with unhelpful police officers and systemic government inability or unwillingness to protect. It discusses the burden placed on applicants to report persecution to authorities before claiming government ineffectiveness, and the tension between this requirement and the acknowledgment that reporting may sometimes be futile or dangerous—particularly in countries with corruption. The post also examines the court's reasoning that evidence of law enforcement searches at the persecutor's property undercut claims of government alignment with the persecutor, and what standard of proof applicants must meet when arguing that reporting would have been pointless.
